name: oe-claude-F-S-P
finalResponse:
# Notes Before the Supply Chain Review

*Written before the steering committee has a name, a template, or a maturity-model spider chart. Resilience programmes that begin with a governance structure tend to produce a governance structure.*

---

## What we're actually buying

The brief asks for resilience and ethical sourcing. Both words have the same problem: they name the outcome we want and quietly assume the thing we'd measure is the thing that causes it.

Resilience gets measured as *number of approved sources* and *weeks of cover*. Ethics gets measured as *percentage of tier-1 spend audited*. All three are procurable in a quarter. A consultancy will sell us the audit coverage, a second-source qualification drive will double the vendor list on paper, and inventory is available to anyone with a balance sheet. If our advantage is any of those, we've bought comfort rather than capacity.

What is not procurable in a quarter: knowing where the material actually originates two and three tiers down; the ability to requalify a part in six weeks instead of eleven months; a supplier who tells us about a problem *before* we find it; and a purchasing rhythm that doesn't itself generate the labour abuses we then audit for.

So I'd let the visible programme be the visible programme — it satisfies the customers, the insurers and eventually the regulators, and it's what our systems can count — and spend the actual effort on sub-tier visibility, requalification speed, our own ordering behaviour, and the price we're willing to pay for honesty. That ordering is the substance of these notes.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

"Various suppliers in multiple countries" is doing a lot of work. I'll write as though we mean a mid-sized manufacturer of electromechanical assemblies: something like 500–700 tier-1 suppliers, spend concentrated in China and Vietnam, secondary flows through Malaysia, Turkey, Mexico and central Europe, and a bill of materials that includes at least one item whose raw input is genuinely opaque to us — a magnet, a wire harness, a moulded part with a mineral filler, a bearing, cotton in the packaging.

If someone in the room knows we're actually a food business, or that 80% of value sits in three suppliers, this is the cheap moment to say it. Most of the structure survives. A good third of the specifics don't.

Worth naming why this is the interesting case. We are large enough to be liable and small enough to be ignored — too small to command a supplier's factory floor, large enough that a detained shipment, an import ban, or a documentary published about a plant we didn't know we bought from will land on us in full.

---

## What our data can and can't tell us

We have a supplier list. We don't have a supply chain map. What we have is an accounts payable file with a географic column, which tells us who we pay and where we send the money — often a trading company, an agent, or a group entity that owns four plants and will decide which one runs our order after the PO lands.

Two things follow, and I'd raise them as questions rather than findings, because procurement will move faster on a conclusion they reach themselves.

**First: is our dual sourcing real?** The most common failure I'd expect us to have is two qualified suppliers, in two countries, on two continents, both buying the same input from the same single plant. Diversification at tier 1 and convergence at tier 3. Nobody designed that. It emerges, because everyone's sub-tier chose the cheapest capable source and the cheapest capable source is usually singular. Worth asking what fraction of our "dual-sourced" A-parts survive a tier-3 test.

**Second: what is our actual constraint in a disruption?** I suspect it isn't finding an alternate. It's qualifying one — the PPAP, the tooling, the customer approval, the regulatory file, the six-week test cycle nobody can compress. If time-to-requalify is eleven months, then no amount of inventory is resilience; it's a delay before the same crisis. If it's six weeks, we can run leaner than we do now. That number, per critical part, is probably the single most useful figure we don't currently hold.

---

## Ideas, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd put these on the table rather than recommend any. Which ones people reach for unprompted tells me more about the organisation than the ideas tell me about the supply chain.

**1. Map by risk, not by spend — a bet on where the exposure actually sits.**
Standard practice maps the top 80% of spend. The parts that stop the line are frequently cheap: a connector, a relay, a specialist coating. I'd propose we rank by *revenue at risk per week of non-supply* and *time-to-requalify*, then go three tiers deep on the top fifty only. Fifty done properly beats six hundred done as a self-assessment questionnaire nobody reads.

The mechanism that works better than asking politely: put sub-tier disclosure in the contract, and where suppliers resist on confidentiality grounds — some resistance will be legitimate — accept disclosure to a neutral third party who holds the map. We don't need to know their margin. We need to know whether their input and their competitor's input come out of the same building.

**2. Pre-qualify and don't buy — a bet on option value over inventory.**
Buying a dormant validated capability is cheaper than buying stock, and it doesn't obsolesce. Concretely: qualify a second source, run a small quantity annually to keep the qualification and the tooling alive, and pay a modest retainer for reserved capacity we hope never to call. Finance will read this as paying for nothing. It's an option premium, and the correct comparison is not to zero — it's to the airfreight, the expedite fees, and the customer penalty we paid last time.

I'd hold inventory where lead time is long and demand variance high, and nowhere else. Blanket weeks-of-cover mandates put stock precisely where it's easiest to hold rather than where it's needed.

**3. Design out the fragility — a bet placed years before procurement gets involved.**
The largest resilience gains available to us are in engineering, and they're currently free of any resilience obligation. Sole-source components are specified at the CAD stage by someone whose objective function is function and cost. Part-count reduction, approved alternates named at design release, avoidance of proprietary single-vendor parts where a standard exists, tolerance bands wide enough that a second supplier can hit them — none of that is a procurement decision, and all of it determines what procurement can do in a crisis.

The uncomfortable implication is that resilience belongs partly in the engineering gate review, with a veto. I'd expect resistance. I'd also expect that resistance to be informative.

**4. Read the signals we already receive and ignore — a bet on early warning being cheap.**
Supplier failure is rarely sudden. It's preceded by things visible from outside: lengthening payment terms to *their* suppliers, receivables factored at rising discount, a trade credit insurer quietly reducing cover, key personnel leaving, a plant running one shift where it ran three. Credit insurers withdrawing cover on a supplier is arguably the best early warning available to us and I doubt anyone here currently receives it as an alert.

Similarly on the ethics side: local labour NGO reporting, port detention data, and strike activity in an industrial park tend to precede an audit finding by a year or more.

**5. Audits are evidence of having audited — a bet on what actually correlates with harm.**
This is the one I'd most want said early, because the programme will otherwise default to buying audit coverage.

An announced social audit measures what a factory permits it to measure. Double books, coached workers, a subcontracted night shift in a building the auditor never sees — the failure modes are well documented and the correlation between audit score and actual worker harm is weak. What correlates better, and is knowable without setting foot in the plant: the proportion of migrant workers, the recruitment corridor they came through, whether pay is piece-rate, the depth of unauthorised subcontracting, and the volatility of the production peaks — which is to say, us.

So I'd propose three moves instead of more audit spend:

- **Worker voice not controlled by either party.** A grievance channel run by a third party, in the languages actually spoken on the floor, with a published response time and no route back to the supervisor who caused the problem. And the success metric is *rising* grievance volume in year one. Falling complaints in a new channel means it isn't trusted. I'd write that into the KPI before anyone reports a decline as progress.
- **Employer Pays Principle, budgeted as unit cost.** Where workers paid recruitment fees to get the job, those fees get reimbursed and future ones borne by the employer. Debt-bonded labour is the most common serious abuse in our likely corridors and it's structurally invisible to inspection. It also costs money, which is why it stays unfixed. I'd rather see it as a line in the standard cost than as a remediation surprise.
- **Traceability to the transformation point, not the tier.** Smelter, mill, gin, refinery. For minerals that means smelter-level lists; for cotton or similar, isotopic or genetic testing rather than paperwork, because paperwork in a mass-balance system is exactly what a determined bad actor produces most readily. This matters commercially as well as morally: an import ban with a rebuttable presumption requires a documentary file *before* the container is detained. Building it afterwards is how a shipment becomes a write-off.

**6. Audit ourselves, and let the suppliers do it — a bet on root cause.**
Much of what we would find in a labour audit, we caused. Late engineering changes, unforecast volume spikes, expedite requests, and price reductions demanded mid-contract all convert directly into unpaid overtime and unauthorised subcontracting. The factory absorbs our irregularity in the only currency it has.

So: a purchasing-practices scorecard where **the supplier grades us** — forecast accuracy, change-order lateness, payment timeliness, expedite frequency — collected by a third party, reported to the board, and attached to the incentives of the people who generate the behaviour. If our own buyers' bonuses depend on an annual across-the-board savings percentage, we are paying people to create the findings we then pay auditors to discover.

**7. Price honesty explicitly — a bet against our own instinct.**
Right now, a supplier who discloses a problem risks losing the business, and a supplier who conceals one usually doesn't. We have, without deciding to, purchased silence. Everything else in this document fails if that stays true.

The proposal: a disclosure protection commitment, in writing. A supplier who self-reports a serious issue and agrees to a remediation plan cannot lose our volume *for the disclosure*. They can lose it for refusing to remediate. And a corresponding responsible-exit protocol — notice periods, an obligation to settle owed wages, no walking away from a facility the week a journalist calls, because cutting and running protects us and abandons the workers, which is the outcome that looks best and is worst.

This deletes a piece of leverage we currently enjoy, and it will be argued against on exactly those grounds. Better to have that argument in month one, in daylight, than in month fourteen when someone quietly reintroduces the threat to hit a cost target.

---

## Sequencing, lightly

I'd resist a three-year roadmap. The situation will move faster than the document.

Something like: the first ninety days on the risk-ranked map and time-to-requalify numbers for the top fifty parts, plus the credit and NGO signal feeds, both of which are close to free. Then the option-value pilot on five parts and the worker voice channel in one corridor, small enough that failure is survivable and instructive. The purchasing-practices scorecard and the disclosure protection can start immediately, because they cost nothing but discomfort. Design-stage requirements enter at the next platform, not retroactively.

On governance: a steering committee will produce reports. I'd rather see three or four people with an actual mandate, an unglamorous budget, and permission to stop a part release — sitting across procurement, engineering and legal, reporting to whoever will genuinely back them rather than to whoever is nominally senior. Authority in this work comes from having read the map, not from the org chart.

---

## What would tell me I'm wrong

If the tier-3 test shows our dual sourcing is genuinely independent, ideas 1 and 2 shrink considerably. If time-to-requalify turns out to be short across the critical set, we're over-inventoried and this is a cost-out exercise, not a resilience one. If the worker voice channel runs a year at low volume in a corridor where local reporting says otherwise, the channel is broken and I'd want to know that rather than celebrate it.

And if the room's energy goes overwhelmingly to audit coverage and dashboard design, that's worth noticing too — not as a criticism, but as information about what we'll actually be able to do.
